title: Enhans, GS Caltex undertake government project to develop AI model based on tacit manufacturing know-how - 디지털투데이
content: Enhans, an enterprise agentic AI company, said on Tuesday it will carry out a project with GS Caltex to develop an AI model based on tacit manufacturing know-how that links skilled workers’ experience and judgement criteria at production sites to data. The research and development is part of the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy’s "2026 AI model development project based on manufacturing tacit knowledge". Enhans will serve as the lead research and development institution and oversee overall development. GS Caltex will participate as the demand company, with OpenGraphLabs as a partner for parsing unstructured documents, and Chonnam National University and GIST participating as joint research institutions. Through the work, Enhans will connect GS Caltex equipment-related structured data, unstructured documents and maintenance history with judgement criteria and exception-handling experience secured through interviews with on-site engineers. It plans to structure relationships such as equipment, parts, abnormal signs, causes and measures based on 832,996 GS Caltex facilities and about 2,900 unstructured documents. It will identify, among engineers in the process, mechanical, electrical and instrumentation fields, the sequence for checking equipment conditions, criteria for narrowing down causes and additional considerations in exceptional situations, and reflect them in the ontology design. The knowledge built will be implemented as a guide chatbot for on-site use. If on-site staff ask questions in natural language about equipment abnormalities or maintenance situations, the system will present candidate causes and inspection sequences. It will also allow them to check original sources that can serve as grounds for judgement, such as past maintenance history and technical standards, the company said. Enhans Chief Executive Lee Seung-hyun (이승현) said it was important to go beyond leaving skilled workers’ experience simply in documents and convert it into knowledge that companies can use continuously. He said the company will build a system that supports on-site staff in checking the information and grounds for judgement they need and resolving problems more efficiently. Team Germany (Men’s) and Team Europe (Women’s) won the 10th BMW Motorrad International GS Trophy, held in Romania September 13-18. The qualifying rounds did not include the USA this year; however, two Americans qualified through the open International Qualifier, held at Enduro Park Hechlingen in Germany last year. Representing the USA on Team International were Stephanie Townsend in the Women’s division and Jordan Wiley in Men’s. This year’s edition was more technical than ever, with narrow forest trails, washed-out mountain paths, riverbeds and high-altitude routes. After six days and approximately 930 miles, Team Germany (Fabi Fenner, Norman Pleissner, Flo Thomann) won the Men’s competition with 203 points, while Team Europe (Chrissie Harcourt and Anja Filak) won the Women’s competition with 200 points. The Women’s competition was decided only in the final challenge, with Colorado’s Townsend and teammate Eduarda “Duda” Mikulski from Brazil on Team International entering the final day ahead of Team Europe by just two points. “We were certainly the smallest team in the competition,” Anja Filak, Team Europe, said. “But we rode like one body, as one unit. Chrissie is amazing. She gave me a lot of advice, and I was able to follow her and make it through. I gained more confidence because I knew I could follow her and stay focused. I took everything she told me over these days very much to heart and tried to put every piece of advice into practice – and it worked!” “I can hardly describe this feeling,” Chrissie Harcourt, Team Europe, said. “My head is a little all over the place; everything feels a bit shaky. It will take a while for it to truly sink in. I am incredibly proud of both of us.” Shifting weather and a midday downpour made for treacherous conditions for the final 75-mile loop and grassy hillclimbs through the narrow mountain ridges and the “Maze,” a technical obstacle course enclosed by ribbons. In the end, Team Europe secured a narrow victory over Team International. With the podium finish, Townsend cements her place in the history books as the highest-placing American woman in the event’s history. The men’s Team International placed seventh. title: IMPC: Samantha Tan recovers through the field before setback ends Indianapolis charge - racers-behindthehelmet.com
content: Samantha Tan endured a mixed IMSA Pilot Challenge outing at Indianapolis, with the Canadian climbing from 24th to 15th in the opening stint before a setback brought her progress to an end and ultimately left the #38 ST Racing by Random Vandals BMW M4 GT4 27th in GS. Samantha Tan endured a mixed IMSA Pilot Challenge outing at Indianapolis, with the Canadian climbing from 24th to 15th in the opening stint before an off-track incident brought her progress to an end and ultimately left the #38 ST Racing by Random Vandals BMW M4 GT4 27th in GS. Tan's first stint had been one of the strongest drives for the #38 BMW, as she made steady progress through the field amid a series of early cautions and was running as high as 15th before the incident forced the car into the pits and left it two laps behind. Bill Auberlen subsequently recovered a handful of positions in the closing stages, but the result could not reflect the pace shown by Tan before the setback. Indianapolis came at the end of a particularly busy period for Tan, who had returned to Europe just one week earlier to compete in the Supercar Challenge at Hockenheim, Germany, making her return to GT3 machinery before heading back to the United States for her primary 2026 campaign in the IMSA Michelin Pilot Challenge GS class. The Canadian stepped up to GS this season, joining Auberlen at ST Racing by Random Vandals in the #38 BMW M4 GT4. Tan had already demonstrated that she could compete with the highly competitive GS field, securing back-to-back top-ten finishes at Laguna Seca and Mid-Ohio, while subsequent outings at Watkins Glen, Canadian Tire Motorsport Park, Road America and Virginia International Raceway had continued to show potential despite mechanical problems and misfortunes preventing the pairing from consistently converting their pace into the results they were targeting. On Saturday Tan took responsibility for qualifying the #38 BMW. She set a 1:31.257 to place 26th in the GS class, leaving the ST Racing by Random Vandals entry to start the two-hour race from 24th in class. Tan made a cautious but clean opening lap, finding herself boxed in through Turn 1 but avoiding the trouble around her. She moved up to 23rd shortly afterwards and became involved in a battle with the #64 CSM Porsche of Houk for position, before fighting her way past Hampton to reclaim 23rd. The first caution arrived after ten minutes when Chaves spun the Toyota Supra into the barriers at Turn 7, triggering a full-course yellow. Tan took advantage of the restart to move into 21st, continuing to make steady progress as the race settled. The green-flag running was again short-lived, however, as the leading TCR entry, the #77 Stallion Motorsports Cupra, suffered a front-suspension failure at Turn 1, immediately bringing out another caution. Racing resumed on lap 13, with Tan continuing her forward progress. A Toyota was tagged into a spin in the middle of the pack shortly afterwards but was able to rejoin without another interruption, while Ward was forced to pit with damage. Tan climbed to 19th as she continued to move forward wth determination. Another major incident involving the #66 Aston Martin and several other cars, including the #46 Team TGM Mustang, brought out a further full-course yellow. Some drivers were forced to take evasive action, once again compressing the field and creating another opportunity for Tan to gain ground. The third restart produced another strong run from the Canadian, who climbed to 17th and continued improving her lap times as the field settled. Tan was soon circulating in the 1:32.5 range and continued to move forward, eventually reaching 15th position. At the 40-minute mark, the first scheduled pit stops were beginning to unfold and Tan initially remained on track, giving the team an opportunity to gain further track position through the strategy. The BMW was therefore in a promising position, with Tan having made significant progress from her starting place and running 15th in class. Unfortunately, the race changed dramatically moments later; the #38 BMW slid through the gravel, bringing out another full-course yellow and ending Tan's strong opening stint. The incident forced the BMW to be towed back to the pits, where Auberlen was able to take over the car, but the time lost during the recovery left the ST Racing entry effectively two laps down and 28th in GS. The race returned to green with 55 minutes remaining, leaving Auberlen with a difficult recovery task. The veteran driver settled into the 1:32s and began working his way back through the field, closing in on Kris Wilson's #64 Ford. Wilson was only around two seconds ahead and Auberlen was almost a second per lap quicker on lap 51. He rapidly closed the gap and completed the pass over the following laps, moving the #38 into 26th position. Auberlen continued to circulate strongly but the deficit left the BMW with limited opportunities to recover further positions. He made his final pit stop with 12 minutes remaining and rejoined in 28th. The race was interrupted once more with five minutes remaining when overall leader Gabby Chaves, who had not yet completed his final pit stop, slowed after running out of fuel and stopped on track, triggering another full-course yellow. Rain was also beginning to appear around the circuit, adding another variable to the final stages. Auberlen was able to gain one further position during the restart, moving into 27th before the chequered flag. The result was ultimately not representative of what had been a very promising first stint for Tan. Starting 24th, she had made her way through a chaotic opening phase of the race and climbed as high as 15th before the incident. Despite the Indianapolis setback, Tan and Auberlen continue to build experience together in Tan's first GS campaign, with the #38 pairing having now collected 1,360 points after nine rounds of the 2026 IMSA Michelin Pilot Challenge season. title: Teradyne Partners With GS Microelectronics On New Semiconductor Test Center — Targets AI, Silicon Photonics And Auto Chips - TradingView
content: Teradyne Inc. (TER) shares rose Tuesday after the semiconductor-testing company announced a multi-year partnership with GS Microelectronics U.S. to establish a new test-and-evaluation center focused on AI and other next-generation chips. The center will combine GSME’s chip design and manufacturing capabilities with Teradyne’s automated test systems, helping customers move more quickly from device evaluation and engineering development to production. GSME will operate a dedicated Teradyne-equipped test floor at its new 42,000-square-foot Silicon Valley headquarters. The facility will support chip developers working across AI, silicon photonics, automotive, power management, and radio-frequency technologies. Customers can use the center for demonstrations, device evaluations, engineering development, pilot production, and technical training, with access to Teradyne's test handlers and probers. The facility is scheduled to open in the fourth quarter of 2026. The partnership also has a commercial component. GSME and Teradyne plan to work together on joint sales engagements, target accounts, technical workshops and customer briefings, with the stated goal of accelerating Teradyne-based design wins and expanding market adoption. GSME is also expanding its test-engineering team across the U.S., Taiwan, Europe and the Gulf Cooperation Council region to support customer programs and application-specific requirements. AI Complexity Is Increasing The Need For Chip Testing As semiconductor designs grow more complex, driven by AI data center buildouts, rapid access to high-performance test development capabilities becomes essential, Teradyne Semiconductor Test Group President Shannon Poulin said. He added that combining Teradyne’s test platforms with GSME’s engineering capabilities is intended to help customers move more efficiently “from development into volume production.” That demand is already showing up in Teradyne’s business. Its Semiconductor Test segment generated a record $1.12 billion in revenue in the fiscal second quarter (Q2), up 128.1% year over year, primarily due to higher AI-related compute and memory sales. Overall Q2 revenue reached $1.33 billion, up 104% from $652 million a year earlier. The company’s semiconductor-testing business hit a record for the second consecutive quarter, driven by continued AI investment across the compute and memory markets. The company also recorded more than $200 million in memory-test revenue for a third straight quarter, supported by demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM) and DRAM testing for AI compute deployments. title: Goldman Eyes Nearly $70B Revenue Base in 2026: What's Driving Growth? - TradingView
content: The Goldman Sachs Group, Inc. GS continues to demonstrate the benefits of the strategic transformation undertaken over the past several years. Speaking at the Barclays 24th Annual Global Financial Services Conference, chairman and CEO David Solomon highlighted that the company expects its revenue base to reach roughly $70 billion this year, up from the mid-$30 billion range when its strategic plan began in 2018–19. The expansion reflects growth across core businesses, a more diversified revenue mix and improving operating leverage. A key pillar of GS’s strategy has been reducing the dependence on more cyclical revenue streams and building a broader and more durable earnings base. The company now centers its growth strategy around two major franchises — Global Banking & Markets (“GBM”) and Asset & Wealth Management (“AWM”). In GBM, Goldman continues to capitalize on its strong positions in investment banking, equities and FICC, while expanding financing activities. In the first half of 2026, Global Banking & Markets revenues climbed 35% to $28.26 billion, led by robust investment banking and Equities activity. AWM is also becoming an increasingly important source of recurring revenues. The business is growing faster than its targeted high-single-digit pace, with roughly $4 trillion in assets under supervision. Goldman is expanding wealth management, alternatives and private credit, while targeting a 30% margin and high-teen returns. Alternatives fundraising is expected to exceed $125 billion in 2026. The company is also benefiting from stronger operating leverage. Management expects roughly 6% revenue growth to translate into a more than 10% earnings increase, supported by scale, automation and productivity initiatives. Continued investments in technology and process redesign could provide further scope for margin expansion. Financial trends underscore this progress. Since Goldman’s first Investor Day in 2020, firmwide net revenues have increased roughly 60%, while more durable revenues have doubled. Momentum strengthened further in the first half of 2026, with firmwide net revenues rising 27% year over year. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for 2026 revenues is pegged at $71.6 billion, indicating year-over-year growth of 22.9% and broadly aligning with management’s expectations for a revenue base of nearly $70-billion range. GS’s push toward a roughly $70-billion revenue base underscores the progress of its multi-year transformation. Growth in Asset & Wealth Management, financing, and other durable revenue streams, combined with ongoing efficiency initiatives, should support stronger earnings growth and improved margins over time. Still, capital-market volatility and elevated investment spending remain key near-term risks. Goldman’s peer JPMorgan JPM and Morgan Stanley MS are also witnessing solid growth in revenues. title: BMW R1300 GS Adventure gets colourful Oktoberfest makeover - Visordown
content: BMW Motorrad has given an R 1300 GS Adventure a colourful Oktoberfest makeover, creating a one-off Wiesn-GS for Munich’s 2026 celebrations. There are few things more German than a GS Adventure, but BMW Motorrad has managed to make its big adventure bike even more Bavarian, thanks to a colourful Oktoberfest makeover. Meet the BMW R1300 GS Adventure x Oktoberfest München 2026, a one-off version of the big GS created specifically for this year’s beer-fuelled celebrations in Munich. Rather than launching another special edition with a few extra accessories and a new badge, BMW has taken an R1300 GS Adventure Triple Black and given it a rather more obvious makeover. The work was carried out with German customisation company ARider, which has covered the bike in a wrap inspired by the official Oktoberfest 2026 poster. The design uses the colours, shapes and graphics from the poster across the GS Adventure’s bodywork, giving it a look that is considerably more colourful than the usually stealthy Triple Black. BMW describes the finished bike as an ‘Unikat’, which is German for one-off. That means this sadly isn't a GS you’ll be able to order from your local BMW dealer. Underneath the Oktoberfest graphics, it remains a standard R1300 GS Adventure. That means BMW’s 1,300cc boxer engine producing 145bhp at 7,750rpm and 149Nm of torque at 6,500rpm, along with the big 30-litre fuel tank that makes the Adventure considerably more touring-friendly than the standard GS. The Triple Black model also brings a substantial equipment list, although BMW’s Oktoberfest project is really about the appearance rather than mechanical changes. There’s no extra power, suspension trickery or performance upgrade hiding underneath the colourful wrap. The project even has its own suitably Bavarian name, with BMW referring to the bike as the ‘Wiesn-GS’. The German manufacturer has also used the phrase ‘Auf’klebt is’’, a play on the Bavarian dialect that refers to the graphics being stuck onto the bike. There’s a competition running alongside the project, too, with BMW Motorrad Germany offering the chance to win a BMW motorcycle for a weekend between 9 and 12 October 2026. title: GS Entec to Supply Substructures for Ulsan Floating Wind Project - en.sedaily.com
content: Signs Agreement With Korean Unit of Sweden's Hexicon GS Entec, the offshore wind substructure unit of GS Group (078930.KS), will take part as a key partner supplying substructures for the Munmubaram floating offshore wind project off Ulsan. GS Entec said on the 22nd that it signed a memorandum of understanding with Munmubaram, the Korean project company of Sweden's Hexicon, to supply mooring pile structures and cooperate on technology for the floating offshore wind farm. The Munmubaram project is a 750-megawatt floating offshore wind development that Hexicon is pursuing in waters about 65 to 80 kilometers east of Ulsan. The plan calls for 50 floating units, taking advantage of strong wind conditions and water depths of 120 to 150 meters. Hexicon has developed and operated 10 floating offshore wind projects in six countries, including the U.K. and Sweden, building up expertise in the field. GS Entec, which is headquartered in Ulsan, will cooperate under the agreement on the fabrication of mooring piles, the exchange of technical information and the establishment of a timely supply chain. The company aims to expand its business portfolio from fixed-bottom monopiles into substructures for floating offshore wind. The company also said it will take the lead in building a mutually beneficial local ecosystem by drawing on Ulsan's shipbuilding and offshore plant industry base. Because floating offshore wind requires a range of equipment including floaters, mooring systems and subsea cables, local companies are expected to gain more opportunities to join the business. title: Robot dances, volleyball autographs and ramyun: inside GS Group's fifth hackathon - 헤럴드경제
content: Employees pitch AI solutions to real workplace problems Photo booths, K-pop robot and signing session add festival feel Record 923 participants; 2,732 have taken part over five years About 30 hackathon ideas already in use at worksites Seven fully deployed, including AI safety platform AIR 'Goal is to redesign inefficient offline work through AI' Some 468 GS Group employees dressed in baseball-style uniforms gathered Monday at the Westin Seoul Parnas in Gangnam-gu for the fifth GS Group Hackathon, spending the day deep in AI solution development. The event looked nothing like a typical stiff corporate AI competition. A photo-booth machine drew a steady stream of participants, while a robot performed K-pop idol dance routines nearby. GS Caltex's KIXX women's volleyball team held an autograph session that had employees lining up to meet the players. Those who needed a break from coding stepped outside to camping chairs, where they ate ramyun by the Han River. The setup was designed to let staff focus on AI development without feeling pressured. GS Group Chairman Heo Tae-soo and GS Caltex Vice Chairman Heo Se-hong attended the event, encouraging employees and asking questions such as how they planned to apply their coding skills. They also visited booths run by participating companies — Amazon Web Services, OpenAI and Hwain Robotics — to ask about the latest technology trends. The hackathon is an annual event where GS Group employees pitch AI-powered ideas to solve real problems inside the company. The two-day event, which runs through Tuesday, is expected to draw a total of 923 participants — 797 from GS affiliates and 126 from outside the group — the largest turnout in the event's history. Cumulative participation over the past five years stands at 2,732. Kim Jin-a, the GS senior managing director who organized the event, said the company pays close attention not just to the ideas employees propose but to the problems they identify. "The agenda that comes up most often at the hackathon is safety," she said, adding that safety workers were spending so much time on paperwork that they had little time to visit actual worksites. Executives are now discussing how to address that problem, she said. This year's theme is "Play with GenAI Season 3: Build & Act" — a signal that the hackathon aims to go beyond idea generation. "Build" means producing AI tools that actually work; "Act" means connecting those tools to real operations and business sites. To help participants, GS provided AI-ready data that AI systems could use on the spot. Kim said there is broad internal consensus that hackathon experiments play an important role in driving change on the ground. "We felt the pace of moving from experiment to real-world application needed to pick up, which is why we chose 'Build & Act' as the theme," she said. About 30 ideas generated through GS hackathons are already being applied at worksites, seven of them fully deployed. The standout example is AIR (AI Risk Assessment), proposed by GS Power employees at the third hackathon. AIR takes a task name and a brief description as inputs and automatically identifies potential hazards, assigns risk ratings and suggests preventive safety measures. The platform is now in use at more than 330 worksites across GS and beyond. A real-time temperature and humidity monitoring alert system being introduced by GS Power, and an AI-based design risk inspection tool at GS Retail, also trace their origins to hackathon proposals. "As the AIR case shows, we are entering an era where employees on the ground can solve problems directly through AI," Kim said. "Starting this year, helping more programs reach actual worksites is our main goal." Underpinning employees' ability to build AI programs with relative ease is Miso, GS Group's in-house AI transformation platform. Used at the hackathon itself, Miso is designed to help staff create AI-related tools without specialized expertise. Kim said employees have used the platform to attempt development of more than 20,000 AI programs. "GS aims to redesign offline work processes through AI," she said. "Certain tasks may be delegated to AI, but that does not mean employees are being replaced." She added that because frontline workers carry heavy workloads, AI handles inefficient tasks on their behalf.

title: GS Group chairman calls for continued workplace innovation through AI tools - 헤럴드경제
content: Chairman Heo Tae-soo attends for second consecutive year 'Not many companies solve field problems through coding,' he says GS Caltex Vice Chairman Heo Se-hong also takes part GS Group Chairman Heo Tae-soo said it represents "significant progress" when frontline employees identify and solve problems on their own using AI — something he said sets GS apart from most companies. "Not many companies around the world directly solve field problems through coding and similar tools," he said. The hackathon is an event where GS employees pitch ideas for boosting workplace productivity and driving other innovations using AI. A total of 923 people are expected to participate through Tuesday, including 797 employees from GS affiliates and 126 outside participants — the largest turnout in the event's history. Cumulative attendance over the past five years has reached 2,732. Heo, who also attended last year's event, has shown a particular affinity for the hackathon. "It is meaningful to see the hackathon grow," Heo said, adding that President Lee Jae Myung praised GS when the two met at Cheong Wa Dae earlier this year. "President Lee already knew about GS's AIR — AI Risk Assessment — and gave us a lot of credit for it," he said. AIR is a safety-management AI agent that originated as an idea at the 3rd GS Group Hackathon in 2024. When a user enters a task name and brief description, the AI automatically identifies potential hazards, assigns risk ratings and suggests preventive safety measures. GS has distributed AIR free of charge to more than 330 worksites, including small and midsize businesses. President Lee praised GS for its contribution to resolving safety issues at smaller companies. Heo said that in the past, employees who needed a digital tool had to submit a request to the IT department and wait for developers to deliver results. "Now, the people who know the field best can build anything they need through AI," he said. He added that ideas generate even greater value when applied and spread across the workplace, and expressed hope that employees would use AI as a basic tool to drive innovation in their work. GS Caltex Vice Chairman Heo Se-hong, who also attended the event, said in his opening remarks that GS must become the company best at solving real-world problems customers face using new technology. "This does not start with sweeping change," he said. "It begins with small attempts — members questioning existing ways of doing things and putting new ideas into action." Heo went on to reference Carrier Pigeon, a slow-messaging app gaining popularity in the United States. The app delays message delivery in proportion to the physical distance between users — if the recipient is on the other side of the world, a message can take days to arrive. "This app offers people worn out by constant notifications and instant communication the pleasure of waiting," Heo said. "In the AI era, what ultimately matters is being clear about whose problems you are solving and what those problems are." He added that AI will advance far more rapidly going forward, and that technologies that seem novel today will soon become ordinary tools anyone can use. "Ultimately, competitiveness comes from internalizing the process of identifying problems and solving them with new technology," he said.

title: "We Don't Call Ourselves an AI Organization": GS Outlines Its Field-Centered AX Strategy - 아시아경제

On the 21st, Jina Kim, Executive Director at GS, outlined the company's AX strategy at the 5th GS Group Hackathon held at Westin Seoul Parnas in Gangnam-gu, Seoul. Rather than simply jumping on the generative AI bandwagon, GS is focusing on identifying real-world problems in the field and connecting them with the most suitable technologies. Jina Kim, Executive Director of GS, is interviewing with reporters at the 5th GS Group Hackathon held on the 21st at Westin Seoul Parnas in Gangnam-gu, Seoul. GS At this year's hackathon, around 250 teams presented problems, and GS is grouping them by cause and reviewing them as company-wide improvement initiatives. Kim explained, "We focus less on the ideas themselves and more on the underlying problems people bring," adding, "For issues that are difficult to resolve at the employee level, we address them by changing the company's systems or processes." Tangible results are also emerging. So far, about 30 ideas generated at the GS Hackathon have been put into practice, with 7 already fully implemented. A prominent example is the safety management AI agent 'AIR' (AI Risk Assessment). Proposed by five employees from GS Power during the 3rd hackathon, AIR has evolved into a service where AI, upon receiving worksite information, identifies risk factors, assigns risk levels, and suggests preventive measures. Currently, 330 companies are using the service. 'Cheki' by GS Retail is another notable outcome of the hackathon. This AI-powered service verifies whether marketing content meets brand guidelines and identifies the presence of hate speech, and has been adopted not only by GS Retail, but also by GS Caltex, GS Engineering & Construction, GS Art Center, and GS Sports. GS is also developing AI specialized for industrial settings. The company is currently collaborating with AI model startups to create AI models tailored to power plants, aiming to support field decision-making by understanding plant schematics, operational data, maintenance histories, and alarms. Kim explained, "We are developing a model that can accurately analyze various issues and alarms that arise at power plants and understand schematics and logic." Kim distanced herself from the view that AI exists to replace employees. She stated, "Our goal is to delegate work to AI, but this does not equate to staff reductions." She emphasized, "AI reshape aims to redesign entire work processes so employees can spend less time on repetitive manual tasks and inefficiencies, freeing them to focus on their core work and field activities." Ultimately, what Kim wants to build is not just technology itself, but "an organization where problems can be voiced." Since 2020, GS has been running the '52g' initiative, which identifies issues in the field and solves them digitally. To date, a cumulative 10,000 people have participated and about 230 projects have been conducted. Kim remarked, "The biggest problem organizations face is being unable or unwilling to open up about field problems," adding, "A culture in which anyone can voice and solve field problems will become the core of GS Group's organizational culture." GS’s hackathon is also expected to evolve into a platform that spreads this culture. Kim even suggested that next year's hackathon may not focus on AI. Instead, the plan is to choose topics—like physical AI or robotics—that are most necessary in the field at that time. "We will ensure it remains a platform where anyone can bring in problems and find access to the best technologies and support to solve them," she concluded. © The Asia Business Daily. title: GS Engineering & Construction builds pre-verification center for construction robots - 헤럴드경제
content: Workers, materials and sequential processes all factored in Construction sites push ahead with physical AI adoption GS Engineering & Construction announced Tuesday that it has established a proof-of-concept center to comprehensively verify the performance and operational viability of new technologies and construction robots before deploying them at actual job sites. The center was created by remodeling part of the company's technology research institute in Yongin, Gyeonggi Province. It goes beyond one-off performance tests of individual robots, providing a dedicated space to identify and address the wide range of variables that can arise when applying technology to the unpredictable conditions of a construction site. Through the proof-of-concept process, the center rigorously examines how workers and robots divide responsibilities, as well as work sequences, movement routes and operating conditions, and puts in place the integrated processes required for real-world deployment. The center is currently running active tests on a range of construction robots, including a concrete leveling robot. The company independently verifies each robot's work accuracy, productivity and site-readiness, focusing on processes that demand both quality and efficiency simultaneously — such as achieving floor flatness after concrete is poured. GS Engineering & Construction plans to evaluate the center's results and utilization before pursuing the opening of additional centers with enhanced capabilities and expanded scale. Unlike a manufacturing factory, where work takes place on a standardized production line, a construction site is a quintessentially unstructured environment in which workspaces, movement routes, personnel and materials shift continuously as each phase of work progresses. For this reason, even the most capable robot will struggle to deliver real productivity gains on site unless it accounts for workers' existing tasks, material delivery and movement paths, and potential interference with preceding and subsequent work phases. That is why GS Engineering & Construction focuses not simply on introducing robots and AI, but on how to integrate those technologies seamlessly into existing construction processes. The company plans to build a virtuous cycle in which technologies are thoroughly reviewed at the pre-verification stage — covering worker fatigue reduction from repetitive-task elimination, quality consistency, safety risk reduction, the feasibility of nighttime and unmanned operations, and linkage with follow-on processes — before being deployed on live sites, with proven technologies then rolled out across other projects. To support this effort, the company also operates an in-house innovation body called the ICC (Innovation Connect Council), which systematically identifies physical AI technologies. Through the ICC, the company pinpoints productivity bottlenecks and technology needs on site, then scouts domestic and international startups and AI and robotics technologies to address them. Where necessary, it pursues joint technology development or investment alongside the proof-of-concept process before applying solutions in the field. In addition, GS Engineering & Construction maintains ongoing exchanges with construction companies, robotics firms and research institutions at home and abroad, sharing practical case studies and know-how on technology application at job sites, while expanding collaboration with overseas companies on technology exchange, promising-technology identification and investment linkages. "The key is not simply bringing robots to a site, but identifying technologies that match the site's actual needs and naturally embedding them into existing construction processes through thorough pre-verification," a company official said. "The ultimate goal is to simultaneously raise productivity, safety and cost competitiveness." Meanwhile, GS Engineering & Construction posted an operating profit of 232.4 billion won ($168 million) in the first half of this year, up 41.8 percent from 164.2 billion won in the same period last year.

title: Ryan Serhant on the Art of Selling Luxury Real Estate - Goldman Sachs
content: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. Goldman Sachs’ weekly newsletter, offering economic and markets analysis from across the firm. Subscribe now. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. The luxury real estate brokerage SERHANT. generates over $1 billion in transactions every month. On Talks at GS, Ryan Serhant, founder and CEO of SERHANT., joins Tucker York, chair of Goldman Sachs Wealth Management, to discuss his transition from the theatre to real estate during the 2008 financial crisis, his video-led sales strategies, and how calculated risks have led to the company’s success. This episode was recorded on July 16, 2026. Ryan Serhant: Selling is a transfer of enthusiasm in whatever it is you're selling, but you've got to make a choice every day, "Today is going to be great, and here's why." Tucker York: I think I've got a couple of pages of introduction of you, Ryan, but we've decided that people here kind of know who you are, Ryan Serhant. Welcome to Goldman Sachs. Ryan Serhant: Thanks so much. Thanks for having me. Let's do this. Tucker York: Okay. A lot of people know who you are. Seen the TV. Know about the business. Know about the social media, all that kind of stuff, who you are today. I'm just interested to go back to kind of like, how did you get to this place? So, grew up in the Boston area. Went to Hamilton College. What about the background informs who we have in front of us today? Ryan Serhant: I was always a storyteller. If you ask my parents what my superpower is, they'll say that Ryan could tell stories. And I don't know why, I think it's just a part of my genetics. And so, that kind of morphed into having an interest in theater. My whole family is in finance, but I was always telling stories. And so, when I moved to New York City 20 years ago this month actually in 2006, that's what I wanted to do. And I wanted to do it on stage. Really, really hard to make money. Ran out of money really, really quick. And then I got my real estate license only because I didn't have to go to one spot every day. I didn't want to wait tables or bartend. I didn't really want to go back to school. And I definitely, definitely did not want to move home with my parents. I went home for that Thanksgiving. It was Thanksgiving of 2008. And I was going through my day and some of the rental clients that I was meeting in Bronx and Harlem and everything. And I just remember looking up, and I have three sisters and two brothers, and everyone was just staring at me. I was like, what? And my little brother goes, "Dude, you've changed." I'm like, "What do you mean? I haven't changed." He's like, "You talk so fast now." Like, "I don't talk fast. You talk slow. Maybe you should move to New York. In a New York minute we got deals to do. I got money to make. Let's go." And so, I think I'm a bit of a product of my environment. You know, New York City is an incredibly intellectually curious ecosystem. And it enables you to shoot for the stars. But it will also provide you the opportunity to bury yourself in the pavement. And I think it gives you the tools to work as hard as you possibly can to build as much as you can. So, to answer your question, I don't think I thought about it that much. I knew theater is what I liked. I liked performing. I liked being in front of the camera. I liked being on stage. And I just hustled and did auditions all day long. I got into a soap opera. Then they killed me. I was a pretty famous hand model for a while. Ryan Serhant: I'm dually talented, man. I was born with two of these babies. I'm very thankful. And so, that paid the rent a little bit. And then it just got to the point where I needed to figure out what to do with my life. I wanted to be successful, and I knew what it was like to be in New York City and not have money. And I never wanted to go back there. Tucker York: When I think about where you've ultimately had huge success on the real estate side, this is a tough business that requires a huge amount of perseverance, rejection, all that. Similar to what you hear about all the acting stories. I came to New York. I didn't get the role, but I kept going, I kept going, I kept going. And it sounds the way you talk about it, it was less about, I wanted to be necessarily an actor. I wanted to have enough money to be able to do something I wanted to do. Ryan Serhant: Yeah, it was-- My dad always told me, "You can quit whenever you want at anything you do, but you're only allowed to quit on your best day." And I've never forgotten that. At the end of the day, you have to do an internal check-in where you tell yourself, was today a day a bad day, a good day, or a great day. And if you don't do that, you're going to blink, and 10 years are going to go by. Right? 15 years are going to go by. And you're going to wake up in a life that you worked really, really hard to get to, that you actually resent. And that can happen really quickly, especially in New York. And so, I made very sure that I say, ready, set, go. And at the end of every day, I know where I am. And so, yeah, you quit on your best day. Tucker York: It's a good call. I'm going to get to, like, the really, really good days that follow this. But 2008 is the time when you decide this acting thing's kind of hard. It's not really going to work. I need to make some money. Kind of like, let's sell real estate at the beginning of the global financial crisis. Ryan Serhant: Yeah. It wasn't really-- I mean, yes. Looking back on it, absolute worst time possible to get into the real estate business. For me, like, I had no money. So, it was summer of 2008. I didn't know what else to do. And so, a friend said, "Get your real estate license. Meet people on Craigslist. And then you'll figure it out." All I had to do was make $2,000 a month, and I didn't have to move home. The day I got my license and started, it just so happened to be the day Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy. And to me, you know, I just thought everyone just loses their job all the time. Like, man, every client I would get. Then they would get fired a month later. And then they couldn't close, and you couldn't get a mortgage. But in retrospect, what ended up happening, because so many people got out of the business, and because I was so ignorant, and ignorance in motion wins all the time over intelligence at rest, I just moved as fast as I could. 82% of all newly licensed agents in the United States quit in the first two years. They try it and they bail because it's too hard. There's no salary. There are no benefits. You eat what you kill. Buyers are liars. And sellers will also lie to you, right? Tucker York: Again, these are the four years before you're on TV. And the reality is, you're, like, incredible. Incredibly focused, all in, cold calling. Doing all that kind of stuff all the time. Is that what made you successful? Ryan Serhant: Not at the beginning. The acting business teaches you the art of rejection. And you have to be able to take 52 punches right in the nose and say, "Thank you, sir, may I have another?" Otherwise, you can't do the bit. You have to move home. But you learn that even though people say, "I don't like you because of your face," you have to keep moving. And for me, the rejection on an apartment was never because of my hair. In fact, my hair was super helpful. Because I have an old man set of hair, but a young boy face, and especially at that time, I would meet clients, and they would look at me, and then they would look up, and they'd say, "How long have you been in this business?" Instead of saying how old are you. And I would just say, "A while." And "a while" is great marketing. So, I did a couple things. One was Craigslist ads. And I would just meet people cold. And I would post ads for apartments and have keys in my pocket and run around. Two was I would just go on the street. The best part about New York was that every single person outside was a potential client. And so, I would stand outside Saks Fifth Avenue because our office was at 20 East 49th. If you had more than two shopping bags, you could probably afford a new apartment. I had business cards back then, old school business cards, and I would say, you know, "My name is Ryan Serhant. If you're looking to buy or sell or rent in New York City, please reach out to me." Some of those people and their families are still clients to this day. Tucker York: You do the hard work during this period of time. And then you catch this gig on TV. Ryan Serhant: Luck is what happens when opportunity meets hard work. And hard work trumps luck when luck doesn't work hard. And so, I'd spent my entire life thinking I was going to do X. And it didn't work out for me. And instead of treating it like a brick wall, which a lot of people do, I treat every obstacle like a speed bump. In the grand scheme of life, it's just a speed bump. Just keep driving. That's what I did when theater didn't work out and got into real estate. I put theater to the side. I put acting to the side. And then there was an open casting call in Times Square for Million Dollar Listing in New York in March of 2010. And I went just because why not? Why would I not go? And I'd done stuff, you know, on camera before. And 3,000 real estate agents showed up. And then they whittled us down over the course of nine months to four of us. They shot the first season of that show with all four of us. And they told us, at the beginning, "Only three of you will make the final cut. So, be good." And so, I just did what I've always done. I just buckled down, and I just grinded, and I knew the one thing that I had was a relentless sense of optimism. Even in our company today, optimism is not a personality trait. It is an operational discipline. Everything can be bad for everybody all the time. There are always ups. There are always downs. But you've got to make a choice every day, today is going to be great, and here's why. And then the show happened, and, you know, ran for 10 years. Tucker York: So, by the way, the optimism thing, too, it's infectious. Ryan Serhant: Selling is a transfer of enthusiasm in whatever it is you're selling. Tucker York: So, you're on TV. The TV helps the real estate, helps the TV, right? Tucker York: Things are going legitimately great for you until we get to the next global crisis, COVID, and you decide, hey, let's end this and start a company. What's the motivation? Is it greed? Is it fear? Ryan Serhant: By 2018, I had the number one residential selling real estate team in New York City history. I had four television shows. I was writing my first book. I had all this stuff that I was doing, and I didn't know what was next. Am I just going to sell real estate? And also, I saw that the world was starting to change. I saw that real estate was moving from being something that was searchable to something that was discoverable. I have never used my company for distribution ever, because in Instagram and in YouTube, where we started doing property tours and promoting real estate at a social level in 2013 and 2014, I could generate more qualified eyeballs for a singular property in ten minutes than any other firm could ever pay for combined. And most people start businesses, I think, completely backwards. They say, "I want to make a profit. How do I make profit? I'm going to create a product. Great. How do I do that? I need people. Okay, why are people going to work for me?" And for me, I did it literally the exact opposite. I have a clear purpose. I'm going to align that with the right people. If you believe in what I'm doing, great. If you don't, you don't have to work for me. We can then sell any product to make all the profit. Tucker York: So, but tell us. Describe SERHANT beyond, if you will. Just the real estate brokerage that it is, but it's other things. Ryan Serhant: Yeah, we have four key businesses. One is the brokerage, which predominantly operates in the cloud. We operate in 17 states. We'll operate in about 25 states by the end of the year. You know, we do about right now just over a billion dollars a month in transactions. We then have Sellit.com, which is our education business. We have Studios, which is our in-house production studio, which is our top of funnel lead generator. So, we create more content for real estate than any other firm on earth combined per month, and we use that to generate organic lead flow. So, our customer acquisition cost is zero. Tucker York: Just because we talked about this before, compare that to other people's customer acquisition cost. Ryan Serhant: You buy them. I mean, you have to buy revenue. Tucker York: The model is to spend millions of dollars advertising stuff, right? Ryan Serhant: Yeah. You advertise to buy customers. And for real estate agents, right, you have to buy them as well. You have to incentivize them to come to you. We buy zero people. We've never bought a single real estate agent ever. People leave tons and tons of money on the table at other firms, and they come to us, and they win with us. I think that's why our agents are the best of the best in the markets that we're in. One of the reasons I also was excited to be asked to be here today, too, is I use the Goldman analogy a lot, right? My interest is not in being the biggest. It is just in being the best. And if I can provide the absolute best service with the best people to the best clients, you can create a pretty great and differentiated company that way. And then they're S.MPLE. S.MPLE is, think of it as, you know, Uber for the home transaction. So, we have technology that empowers the driver who are agents. My goal is to build a transaction platform that is consumer-facing that grabs that $400 trillion total addressable market, right? In the only AI vertical way that you've ever been able to create. I mean, the technology that we have today will solve the greatest problem I've ever had as a real estate agent, which is, how do I take 129 steps and put it in one thing to get a home sold? And you just could never do it until, like, nine months ago. Tucker York: People-intensive business, relationships will still matter, I assume. Ryan Serhant: Yes. Yeah, it doesn't replace trust. I sold a house, a series of houses, last year for $308 million. The most expensive residential transaction in all of 2025 in the United States to somebody very much in the AI space. And he was very, very interested in sales as a skill set that is irreplaceably human. Tucker York: He was studying your Jedi mind tricks. Ryan Serhant: Yeah, my goal with AI, and I think everyone's goal, is how do you superpower human skill so that you can do what you do best and you can actually have more time to build those relationships and build that trust with your clients. Tucker York: Comments about the real estate market today. I find that real estate people say, "Oh, this is the best time to buy and it's the best time to sell," right? Ryan Serhant: Always. Everyone's business is great until it's not. And so, when it rains, grab your buckets. And we are definitely in a bifurcated housing market. And I hardly ever actually use the phrase "housing market" because I really do think we have a housing obstacle course in this country with how difficult and kind of friction the process is. But you have people who can pay cash and you have everybody else. And it used to have parity. Because you have people who would pay cash because they could, but then it was easy and relatively inexpensive to get a mortgage. For the past four years, it has not been so. Inventory is at all-time-lows, year after year after year. But you're starting to see some of that wake up. People have life changes and they adjust to a new normal, which is happening now. Transaction volume is high. The super luxury market is incredibly high. There are massive transactions that are happening all over the country. The first-time home buyer market is incredibly well funded by their parents. So, they've been doing a great job as well. And we continue to move forward. You know, we don't have a housing crisis. We have a housing supply issue. We just have to create more supply. We have to create tax credits. We do commercial now at our company, which is really interesting. So, you're starting to see municipalities start to release kind of derelict office buildings, space they don't have, which is great for the repurpose into residential space. And so, we're doing a lot of that too, to try to do our part to solve the problem. Tucker York: So, we're a large company, we've been around for a long time. And there's a big mentorship culture here and people that have been around here for a long time. Tucker York: And the people that have been around here for a long time also knew it was like when they came in. And so, it's a pay it forward kind of thing. You didn't really have that experience. You're kind of self-taught. Who are the people that kind of help you? How do you get that input? Ryan Serhant: When I started, I had none at all. Everyone told me not to get into real estate. Everyone told me not to do Million Dollar Listing. Everyone for sure told me not to start my own company. And I went the exact opposite way. I have a lot of great clients, incredibly successful clients, that I can call at any time and ask them for advice. But also, I'm only ever going to catch myself. Like I've got to stare at myself in the mirror every day. And so, I'm the one who's going to take the risk. And if things go well, it's because of everybody else. And if things go poorly, it's 100% my fault. And that's the deal I made with myself when I came to New York City. And that's the deal I made with myself when we started the company. You know, my ambition when I first came to the city was, let me figure this out. I've got to try it. I'd rather regret the things I did than the things I never tried. Let's move. Today, I think people confuse my ambition with responsibility. Because if you knew how many other people really win when I win, you'd understand that it's not for Ryan. It's for everybody else. I surround myself with people far smarter than me every single day. I hire intrapreneurs. So, the same way if you're ever building a team or anyone here who's hiring, you want to hire people that, one, make you a little bit afraid because they're so good and they're going to take your job. Otherwise, why work with them? And two, that you're going to be able to really, really, you know, learn from. Tucker York: What's the advice? What's the kind of the learnings in the last 20 years, what you've done, everything else you would share with people, sort of more broadly as they think about career? Ryan Serhant: My go-to is always to take care of the work. And if you take care of the work, the work will take care of you. I meet a lot of people who are very, very outcome focused, which I think is okay. It's good. But really just focusing on, like, well, I've got to get to here and here and here and here, you lose sight of why you're doing the work in the first place. And I think just doing really, really great work day in and day out, if you do that, you will be as successful as you want to be. As long as you move quickly. Speed to lead is a real thing, especially today. As well as taking calculated risks with yourself, with your career. Like, what's the worst that can happen is something that I'll always try to ask myself too. I don't know if that's great advice. But life finds a way. Tucker York: That's your point. Is if you keep working, the odds of that happening are greatly reduced, right? Ryan Serhant: I remember when I first got into real estate and I was running around, I had holes in my shoes, I was exhausted, I was sweaty all the time. And I remember my parents came and visited me in my apartment. And I was complaining about how early I have to wake up, and I'm tired, and this, that, the other. And I remember my dad saying to me, "Do you think that I wanted to go to work every day?" And that sentence, like, blew my mind, you know? Because I grew up with him at State Street in 1993. Like, of course he wanted to go to work. Like, that's what he does. He was Mr. Finance, you know? And so, I knew in that moment, like, okay, I will not complain ever again, and I will just take care of the work, and I will just continue to move forward. Tucker York: Thank you very much for coming to Goldman Sachs and, frankly, sharing a story that I know we all find pretty inspirational and pretty cool. Tucker York: Very successful. Thank you everybody. title: Unveiling Microbial Communities And Biogeochemical Cycles In Antarctic Colored Snow - Astrobiology Web
content:
[BMC Microbiology].   Snow cover, the extensive terrestrial habitat in Antarctica, sometimes exhibits vivid coloration, yet the structure and function of its microbial communities remain poorly characterized. Using metagenomic sequencing of red snow (RS) and green snow (GS) from the Fildes Peninsula, we found that bacterial, eukaryotic, and archaeal relative abundances were 85.82%, 13.52% and 0.16%, respectively. β-Diversity differed significantly between RS and GS across these three domains (P < 0.05). Dominant bacterial phyla included Bacteroidota (RS: 62.61%; GS: 38.72%) and Pseudomonadota (RS: 32.80%; GS: 54.10%). Among eukaryotes, Chlorophyta (RS: 58.10%; GS: 52.98%) and Basidiomycota (RS: 14.80%; GS: 8.08%) were prevalent. Nanobdellota dominated archaea, with lower abundance in RS than GS. In the algal community, Sanguina, Gonium and Chloromonas were significantly enriched in red snow, while Chlorella and Micractinium were enriched in green snow (P < 0.05). Marker genes associated with carbon (C), nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P) and sulfur (S) cycles were identified in green and red snow. Aerobic respiration and phosphate regulation were significantly enriched in red snow, while CO oxidation, fermentation, and denitrification were significantly enriched in green snow. Key microbial genera associated with these functional pathways also varied. In the denitrification of red snow, Stutzerimonas was the most abundant genus, while Janthinobacterium was abundant in green snow. Nitrification-related genes were detected only in red snow based on the present metagenomic data. The network of the red snow microbial community was potentially more complex and resistant based on topology, which not only benefited its own long-term survival but might also have potentially influenced the positive feedback effect of snowmelt by maintaining a low-albedo snow surface. This provided an ecological implication under climate warming: the expansion of red snow patches showed the potential to the increase nitrate runoff export, which would affect nitrogen nutrient levels in coastal Antarctic waters. Overall, this study used metagenomics to compare the multidomain (bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes) composition and diversity between red snow and green snow, and directly linked key microbial taxa with functional genes of biogeochemical cycles. This study provided new insights into the biological characteristics and functional potential of Antarctic colored snow.               send an e-mail Colțești, Romania. After six days of riding, around
  1,500 kilometres and an exceptionally demanding route through the
  Romanian Carpathians, the tenth BMW Motorrad International GS Trophy
  has been decided. Team Germany (Fabi Fenner, Norman Pleissner, Flo
  Thomann) won the men’s competition with 203 points, while Team Europe
  (Chrissie Harcourt, Anja Filak) prevailed in the women’s competition
  with 200 points. The anniversary edition went farther, higher and was
  more technical than ever before – across narrow forest trails,
  washed-out mountain paths, riverbeds and historic high-altitude
  routes. At the same time, it remained true to what defines the GS
  Trophy: a shared adventure in which team spirit, precision, endurance
  and mutual support matter more than outright speed. The outcome was decided only in the final challenge. Ahead of the
  last day, just two points separated Team International and Team Europe
  in the women’s competition, while Team Germany defended an
  eleven-point lead over Team Europe in the men’s competition. Under
  maximum pressure, the eventual winners demonstrated precisely the
  qualities that defined this GS Trophy: trust, composure and consistent teamwork. In the women’s final, Chrissie Harcourt from Great Britain and
  Anja Filak from the Netherlands rode with control and close
  coordination to secure victory for Team Europe. Team Germany,
  comprising Fabian Fenner, Norman Pleissner and Florian Thomann,
  crowned a consistently strong performance throughout the week with
  overall victory in the men’s competition. BMW Motorrad International GS Trophy 2026 Romania – Final standings.

Women’s teams:
1. Europe – 200 points2. International – 1843.
  Australia – 1644. China – 1595. Germany – 146 Men’s teams:
1. Germany – 203 points2. Europe – 1473. Ukraine –
  1444. Australia – 1385. Japan – 1356. Korea –
  1317. International – 1288. China – 102 The winners of the women’s competition, Team Europe, had not known
  each other before this event: one came from Wales in the United
  Kingdom, the other from the Netherlands. Over the course of the event,
  they grew together as a team and, with mutual support, overcame every
  obstacle on their way to victory. Chrissie Harcourt, Team Europe: “I can hardly
  describe this feeling. My head is a little all over the place;
  everything feels a bit shaky. It will take a while for it to truly
  sink in. I am incredibly proud of both of us.” Anja Filak, Team Europe: “We were certainly the
  smallest team in the competition. But we rode like one body, as one
  unit. Chrissie is amazing. She gave me a lot of advice, and I was able
  to follow her and make it through. I gained more confidence because I
  knew I could follow her and stay focused. I took everything she told
  me over these days very much to heart and tried to put every piece of
  advice into practice – and it worked!” The tenth edition set new benchmarks: six days, around 1,500
  kilometres and approximately half of the route away from paved roads.
  For three consecutive days, the teams spent eleven to twelve hours on
  the move; day three featured more than 300 kilometres, including 170
  kilometres of trails. Cold temperatures, dense fog, wet camps and
  constantly changing terrain made recovery and personal organisation
  just as important as riding skill. The most formidable challenges awaited high in the Carpathians: the
  eight-kilometre Metzeler Enduro Navigation Challenge on narrow single
  trails, the uncompromising climbs to the Strategica Mountain Road and
  an exposed descent along a narrow goat track. Riverbeds, deep fine
  gravel, wet grassy slopes and washed-out forest tracks added to the
  challenge. The combination of distance, technical difficulty,

title: RBI sells Rs 25,000 cr govt securities in second OMO tranche to drain surplus liquidity - PSU Watch
content: Mumbai: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Monday accepted bids worth Rs 25,000 crore in the second tranche of its open market operation (OMO) sale of government securities, as it stepped up efforts to absorb surplus liquidity from the banking system. The RBI accepted Rs 11,512 crore of the 6.10 per cent GS 2031, Rs 8,758 crore of the 7.95 per cent GS 2032, Rs 2,300 crore of the 6.75 per cent GS 2029, Rs 2,250 crore of the 7.17 per cent GS 2030, and Rs 180 crore of the 7.17 per cent GS 2028, according to the release. However, the Central bank did not accept any bids for the 8.28 per cent GS 2027, the release said. The OMO sale comes amid a large liquidity surplus in the banking system. Liquidity surplus was estimated around Rs 6.05 lakh crore as of September 20, according to the RBI data. Under an OMO sale, banks and other investors pay the RBI for the government securities, thereby draining rupee liquidity from the banking system. The central bank had announced OMO sales totalling Rs 1 lakh crore in three tranches to manage the prevailing liquidity conditions. The remaining last tranches of Rs 25,000 crore is scheduled for September 28. The banking system was flushed with liquidity due to heavy mobilisation of FCNR (B) deposits by banks, as the mobilisation brought foreign currency into the system, while subsequent swaps with the RBI provided rupee liquidity to banks. Besides FCNR(B) inflows, month-end government expenditure, including payments toward salaries and pensions, also added to liquidity in the banking system. title: Six days, 1500 kilometres and a GS Trophy podium for Australia - MCNews
content: From the wide-open spaces of Mongolia in 2018 to the New Zealand adventure of 2020, MCNews has followed the BMW Motorrad International GS Trophy through some spectacular country. Subsequent editions took the event to Albania in 2022 and Namibia in 2024, before Romania’s Carpathian Mountains supplied the setting for the tenth edition in 2026. And Romania made them work for it. Six days, approximately 1500 kilometres, cold mornings, wet camps and a succession of steep climbs and awkward descents culminated in a rain-affected finale, with Australia’s women claiming third overall and the men finishing just outside the podium in fourth. Germany won the men’s competition, while the European pairing of Chrissie Harcourt and Anja Filak took the women’s honours. Both titles remained in play heading into the final day, despite the much larger margins in the completed standings. The terrain gave the event a very different character from its previous outing in Namibia. Narrow forest trails, washed-out tracks, slippery grass and exposed mountain paths tested the competitors aboard BMW’s R 12 G/S, with roughly half the distance covered off-road. Australia finished the women’s competition on 164 points, five clear of China and 18 ahead of Germany. Team Europe topped the standings with 200, followed by Team International on 184. In the men’s competition, Australia’s 138 points left the team six behind third-placed Ukraine and nine behind runner-up Europe. Japan was only three points further back, underlining how closely the positions behind the winning Germans were contested. Germany’s Fabian Fenner, Norman Pleissner and Florian Thomann finished on 203 points, eventually stretching their advantage over Europe to 56. That final margin disguises a much tighter contest during the week: Germany had entered the last day with an 11-point lead. The 2026 theme was “Back to Basics”, reflected in the choice of the R 12 G/S and an event that placed a premium on bike control, navigation and cooperation. Time mattered in the special tests, but so did accuracy, keeping feet on the pegs and working effectively with team-mates. As detailed in our look at the GS Trophy Competition Bike, the R 12 G/S followed the R 1300 GS used in Namibia and the R 1250 GS ridden in Albania. The air/oil-cooled 1170 cc boxer was equipped with 21-inch front and 18-inch rear wheels, off-road protection and the Enduro Package Pro. Romania put that equipment to use. For the first three days, each rider kept the teams moving for 11 to 12 hours, making fatigue, drying gear, and finding time to recover part of the challenge. Any notion of a gentle introduction disappeared on day one. The Welcome Trial took place on an exposed mountain plateau, where wet grass, off-camber slopes and a steep ascent and descent immediately tested balance and line choice. Putting a foot down, stopping or straying outside the marked course attracted penalties, while the clock added another consideration. The challenge was carrying enough momentum without losing control. The route covered 310 kilometres, including around 150 kilometres of unsealed mountain and forest tracks. The Akrapovič Riverbed Challenge added embankments, soft river deposits and fine gravel to the mix. By late afternoon, there were still 120 kilometres to go, around half of them on technical tracks. The teams finally reached Sighișoara shortly after 6.30 pm, almost 12 hours after setting out. The next morning began at 6°C in dense fog, followed by more than 11 hours of riding through forest sections littered with sand, mud, tight hairpins and deep ruts. Three consecutive climbs provided one of the day’s sternest examinations. The reward at the top was a view across the Carpathians towards the 22.5-metre Sacred Heart of Jesus statue. Near Valea Zălanului, the route mixed flowing forest tracks with river crossings and alternating stretches of gravel and grass across the floodplain. Riders repeatedly had to adjust to different surfaces and grip levels. Day three delivered another cold, foggy start and another itinerary exceeding 300 kilometres, around 170 of them off-road. Damp kit and limited recovery time were becoming familiar companions. The route climbed into the Tătaru Mountains and onto the high pastures of Tabla Buții, a historic ridge route that once marked a national border and later saw fighting during the First World War. The key riding test was the eight-kilometre Metzeler Enduro Navigation Challenge near Zărnești. Following a GPS track through the forest sounds straightforward enough, until narrow single trails, easily missed junctions and steep embankments are added to the equation. With fatigue accumulating, this ranked among the most technical sections of the entire event. Bran Castle, associated with the Dracula legend, provided a memorable landmark towards the end of the day. After three very long days, a 180-kilometre itinerary offered some relief on paper. The riding still demanded plenty. Sleep had already been interrupted by the guard dogs of nearby shepherds, which kept potential wildlife away from the campsite. A trial on a wet, steeply sloping grass field then ensured everyone was properly awake. The route initially flowed towards the Transfăgărășan before two difficult off-road climbs raised the workload again. One demanded precise positioning within a confined space; the other followed a deeply rutted double track along the mountainside, where maintaining traction was critical. The Lotru Riding Challenge finished the competitive programme with a comparatively fast run through rock fields and deep fine gravel in the riverbed. By 4.30 pm the test was complete, finally leaving a little more time for recovery and catching up with the other teams. The fifth day covered more than 300 kilometres back to base camp in Colțești, with the Strategica Mountain Road at its centre. Built as a military road during the First World War, the high-altitude route combined spectacular scenery with steep, technical climbs. Failed attempts could require difficult recoveries, and reaching the top did not signal the end of the hard work. The descent followed a narrow, exposed mountain trail that demanded absolute concentration. Further climbs and steep descents eventually brought the riders to the winding Transalpina, providing a spell on asphalt before more tracks led back towards camp. The final morning began with a 120-kilometre loop, evenly divided between sealed roads and unpaved tracks along mountain ridges. Heavier rain then interrupted proceedings, leaving increasingly wet ground for the climbs leading to the last special test. Its two-part layout began with a faster passage across off-camber grass before tightening into a technical section of steep embankments and rock steps. Only two points had separated Team International and Team Europe in the women’s standings before the final day. Harcourt, from Great Britain, and Filak, from the Netherlands, delivered under pressure to secure the title for Europe. The pair had not known each other before the event, making their ability to develop an effective partnership over the six days a particularly fitting GS Trophy success story. “I can hardly describe this feeling. My head is a little all over the place; everything feels a bit shaky. It will take a while for it to truly sink in. I am incredibly proud of both of us.” “We were certainly the smallest team in the competition. But we rode like one body, as one unit. Chrissie is amazing. She gave me a lot of advice, and I was able to follow her and make it through. I gained more confidence because I knew I could follow her and stay focused. I took everything she told me over these days very much to heart and tried to put every piece of advice into practice – and it worked!” Germany also completed the job in the men’s competition, with Fenner, Pleissner and Thomann converting their overnight advantage into the overall win. GS Trophy marshal Matei Albulescu played a central role in bringing the event to his home country, helping scout the route and working with landowners and authorities to secure access. Tabla Buții and Strategica were among his personal favourites, and they helped give the anniversary edition its distinctive mix of history, remote terrain and demanding riding. Even the scoring stayed deliberately simple: marshals assessed the specials with pen and paper, calculated results by hand, and updated the leaderboard each evening. Those numbers ultimately put Germany and Europe on top. For Australia, a women’s podium and fourth in the men’s standings capped six demanding days in a host country that gave the GS Trophy’s tenth edition plenty to remember. title: "It's a Total Hero Ski:" Testers Pick the Best Carving Skis of 2027 - skimag.com
content:
