This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy Overview: The carving ski category is shifting: rather than narrow race-inspired sticks, most 2027 standouts run wider underfoot with more rockered tips, so lesser experts can access that locked-in, arcing feel once reserved for ex-racers. SKI tested this year’s carving skis at Deer Valley, Utah, scoring each on edge hold, hard-snow feel, and control at speed. The seven skis listed in this guide rose to the top of the pile. The carved turn is making a comeback, and this year’s top carving skis have met the moment. A good carving ski initiates a turn, holds it like a cornering sports car, and releases into the next turn. These are directional skis, designed to be skied forward and driven down the fall line. Versatility off-piste is not this category’s jam. It’s all about the turn—your turn. Traditionally, we’ve thought of carving skis as skinny skis with 60-millimeter waist widths. But these days, carving skis come in all shapes and sizes. Those 68-millimeter, dumbed-down World Cup skis still exist, and they’re excellent carvers—but they’re not exactly approachable to the masses. So for this season, we focused our testing on the carving skis that better serve the everyday skier, not just the ex-racers: skis with wider waists and more tip rise to make them friendlier and easier to turn, but no less capable of slicing and dicing up groomers. When SKI’s testers clicked into the bindings of this season’s fleet of carvers in Deer Valley, Utah—a resort renowned for its perfectly manicured runs—they carved up a storm to determine how each ski performed on groomed terrain. When judging the best carving skis, we prioritize hard-snow integrity, carving, and stability at speed, and the seven winners excelled in these areas while nailing performance characteristics across all categories. If you haven’t tried a carving ski, there’s never been a better time to join the movement. And if you’re a tried-and-true carver, this season you’re in for quite a ride: the best carving skis of 2027 are more approachable and exciting than ever. Of the 26 carving skiss we tested at our annual SKI Test in Deer Valley, Utah, these seven stood out as top performers. They earned the highest marks across nine scoring criteria, with especially strong results in carving, hard-snow performance, and stability at speed—the three performance characteristics we prioritize when reviewing carving skis. Read more about our testing process here. Lengths: 163, 168, 173, 178, 183 cm
Dimensions: 123-80-112 mm Pros and Cons
+ Easy to lay over
+ Dependable and trustworthy at speed
– Expensive
– Unforgiving for less aggressive skiers Think of the “A” in the Montero AX as a letter grade, because this Stöckli received summa cum laude honors at our test in Deer Valley, Utah. As “Best in Test,” the Montero AX earned the highest marks in the carving category for hard-snow integrity and stability at speed, proving why this carryforward model is a perennial favorite. “Amazing edge hold and acceleration out of the turn,” said Jon Sexauer, a Colorado-based expert tester. “It’s a strong carving ski that lets advanced and expert skiers arc turns of all shapes and sizes in any snow condition.” Perhaps “all-mountain carver” best captures the Montero AX’s priorities. The visible S-shaped notches in the aluminum over the tip and tail help make turn initiation easier, while full edge contact and camber underfoot let expert skiers lay over and arc turns at cruising speeds. True, the Montero AX is more maneuverable than some Stöckli models, but less aggressive skiers may still find the strong build unforgiving. “It’s a stellar choice for those who can bend a ski but don’t want a gnarly, stiff race ski,” said Tommy Flitton, a Utah-based ski coach. “If you appreciate a smooth, approachable race-ski feel, this is amazing.” Lengths: 152, 160, 168, 176, 184 cm
Dimensions: 132-84-120 mm Pros and Cons
+ Snappy and fun all-mountain carver
+ Approachable for intermediates
– Unforgiving if you get in the backseat
– Tight turn radius resists long turns With the snappiness of Indiana Jones’ whip, the Rossignol Arcade 84 can accurately arc up corduroy or carve through cut-up snow. High scores for carving, quickness, hard-snow integrity and responsiveness won the Arcade 84 the “Most Versatile” award at our test in Deer Valley for its amazing blend of skills. “This Rossi ate up groomers, held a sharp edge on firm snow, and absolutely trenched in soft snow,” said Jon Sexauer, a Colorado-based tester. With a slightly wider waist than other skis in this category, the Arcade 84 balances high-performance precision with all-mountain approachability. A game-on construction—with a full layer of Titanal and a central power rail running down the wood core—is tamed by a curvy sidecut and voluminous, rockered tip. Testers were impressed with the easy turn initiation, as well as its ability to access high edge angles. Though quick and snappy in short turns, long turns take more effort, testers observed. And if you get in the backseat, you might get whipped. But if you can tip the Arcade 84 over and drive it down the fall line, you’re in for an adventure. Lengths: 161, 168, 175, 182 cm
Dimensions: 126-76-109 mm Pros and Cons
+ Terrific stability at speed and long-radius turns
+ Super snappy and reactive
– Lacks forgiveness in variable conditions
– One-trick pony So intuitive is the Fischer The Curv Noize GTX that testers called it a mind reader. It initiates turns seamlessly at the merest touch of pressure, earning it the highest scores in the test for carving ability. “All it wants to do is lay over on edge and absolutely trench,” said Jon Sexauer, a Colorado-based tester. “It feels so supportive and stable that you have unlimited confidence to drive it hot lap after hot lap.” Best for strong intermediates through experts, the Curv Noize GTX has a metal-and-wood core construction with Noize Control Tech—3D-printed particles placed along the length of the ski to help absorb vibrations and “quiet” it. A carbon-fiber wrap adds torsional stiffness and responsiveness. The result? “It makes groomers entertaining,” said Alex Cernichiari, a 5-foot-10 expert skier. “It can bring you out of a turn and into the next one at slow to moderate speeds, but at higher speeds, it can hold an edge perfectly.” Though versatile in turn shape and speed preference, the 76-millimeter-waisted ski does have a one-track mind and a groomer zip code: “Carve, carve, carve is all it thinks about,” quipped Todd Casey, a Colorado-based ski instructor. Testers gave it low marks in forgiveness and playfulness, citing its reluctance to do anything else. But if arcing up groomers is your idea of a great time, the Curv Noize GTX doesn’t disappoint. Lengths: 156, 163, 170, 177 cm
Dimensions: 125-76-109 mm Pros and Cons
+ Nimble, agile and approachable
+ A blast to make turns on
– Light construction means less reliable at speed
– So turny it can be fatiguing As the TikTok dancer of skis, the Salomon Addikt 76 has great moves. Case in point: it earned top scores in quickness, responsiveness and playfulness. “It’s a total hero ski,” said Avery Pesce, a Utah-based expert tester. “Not only does it have super easy turn initiation and stability at high speed, but it provides insane rebound energy out of the turn.” Like sequined pants, Salomon’s Motion Tail Technology catches the eye. The cutout in the swallowtail is designed to increase tail flexibility and turn release. Polymer pads in the metal layer add liveliness, while the shapely sidecut invites responsiveness and snap out of the turn. You don’t have to be a pro to access the Addikt 76’s talents: testers recommend this approachable ski for experts down to timid intermediates, since it can pivot and make short-to-medium-sized turns, as long as the emphasis is on “turn.” “It can get a bit fatiguing if you’re making that many energetic turns on bigger, longer runs,” said Lauren Engle, a 5-foot-4 expert skier. “But for skiers in the East and Midwest, where runs are shorter and narrower, this ski can make those conditions a blast.” Some testers noted that the swallowtail and lighter construction reduced reliability on very firm snow at speed. Icy runs aside, if workout skiing is your jam, and your ski studio has grippable groomers, the Addikt 76 will make a great partner. Lengths: 165, 170, 175, 180 cm
Dimensions: 131-82-112 mm Pros and Cons
+ Approachable and confidence inspiring
+ Very responsive and locks in on long radius turns
– Lacks some stability at high speed
– Sluggish to transition between short and long turns If the Blizzard lineup were beer styles, the Firebird would be the high-octane IPA, and the Stormbird 82 DTI would be the lager—medium-bodied, low-octane, and more popular among the masses. It’s not a watered-down race ski, but it has race-like characteristics with a flex profile that makes it more approachable for non-racers. Testers were impressed with how the Stormbird 82 DTI inspired confidence on the groomed slopes of Deer Valley, scoring it high marks across all criteria, most notably quickness, carving, and responsiveness. Though capable of making short-radius turns, the Stormbird 82 DTI is happiest skiing wide-open runs, locking into long turns on firm snow with strong tip-to-tail edge hold. This iron edge grip can also make the 82-millimeter-waisted ski feel sluggish transitioning between long and short turns, but according to testers, it just requires patience. The Stormbird 82 DTI (with dual Titanal layers) has a race-heritage construction, but the flex profile is the secret sauce. With a stiffer flex in the center, medium flex around the binding, and softer flex in the tip and tail, “you don’t feel like you’re working to bend the ski every turn, but you have energy and engagement at a moment’s notice,” said Otto Gibbons, a Washington-based ski buyer. “That nimbleness and softness makes it approachable for a huge range of skiers.” Lengths: 153, 160, 167, 174, 181 cm
Dimensions: 127-75-110.5 mm Pros and Cons
+ Good balance of energy and stability
+ Grips and rips like a GS carving ski
– Can be stiff underfoot for less aggressive skiers
– Bouncy at the tip at speed Atomic’s new Redster Q collection showcases World Cup technology paired with components that level the playing field for non-racers. As a new addition to the family, the Redster Q9 Revoshock S widens that field even further. As tester Jon Sexauer, a Colorado-based expert skier, described it, “This is a no-nonsense carver for any turn shape that can be pushed by aggressive skiers, but still remains approachable for less aggressive skiers developing their technique.” At 75 millimeters underfoot, it’s no shock that testers awarded the Redster Q9 Revoshock S high marks for hard-snow integrity, describing it as “a BFF for crushing corduroy.” Beyond groomers, testers were impressed by its ability to steer and skid easily between different snow conditions without a lot of rattle. This stability comes from the built-in stainless-steel suspension system called Revoshock S—the same technology that smooths out gnarly race-course ruts. There’s also a Carbon Boost inserted behind the heel, providing power and acceleration out of the turn, resulting in “a nice balance of energy and stability,” according to Nick Loomans, a 6-foot expert skier. “It’s like a GS carving ski that’s versatile and nimble enough to perform other types of turns, too.” Less aggressive skiers should look to the Redster Q7, built with carbon Revoshock instead of steel, because testers found the Q9 Revoshock S rather stiff underfoot. But for go-getters, the Q9 is the carver you can attack the fall line with. Lengths: 146, 152, 160, 168, 176 cm
Dimensions: 132-84-120 mm Pros and Cons
+ Initiates turns easily
+ Fun and easy to maneuver
– Has a power limit if overloaded
– Rebound energy can be off-putting Whether you’re an intermediate working on perfecting your carved turn or an instructor working on your exam maneuvers, the Rossignol Arcade W 84 is a frontside-adjacent carving ski with exceptional maneuverability. That’s the point of this 84-millimeter-waisted ski: to blend approachability with high-performance, a recipe that impressed testers across all scoring criteria, particularly in carving and quickness. “There’s not a resort skier out there on either coast that wouldn’t have fun on this ski,” said Avery Pesce, VP of merchandising at Boston Ski and Tennis. “It has so much lively energy for short turns on the side of the trail and great smoothness and stability in longer radius turns on hardpack.” The Arcade W 84 has a full-on wood and metal construction, complete with a central power rail running down the center. Add in the extended sidecut, big rockered tip and vibration absorption—a throughline from the Temptation to the Arcade line—and you get a dynamic ski that loves to arc quick turns. If you prefer a damper ski without a lot or rebound energy, look elsewhere. “The edge-to edge energy can be a lot if you’re not used to pop into the next turn,” noted Courtney Harkins, a 5-foot-8 expert skier. “Overload them too much and their incredible energy will slingshot you across the hill.” But harness the Arcade W 84’s energy, and this people-pleasing ski will oblige. The following carving skis are models that excel in specific areas like playfulness or forgiveness, offering strong alternatives for skiers with specific performance preferences. Lengths: 162, 167, 172, 177, 182 cm
Dimensions: 126-80-109 mm Pros and Cons
+ Smooth and stable
+ Reliable edge grip
– Tail can be sluggish to release
– Not as lively as some The Völkl Peregrine 80 impressed our testers with its silky-smooth feel, turn-shape versatility and edge hold, ranking it among the best in stability and hard-snow integrity. An effort to reduce weight made it more approachable, according to testers, without giving up much in return. “A Völkl with less weight? Sign me up!” quipped Otto Gibbons, hardgoods supervisor for Sturtevants Ski Mart. “The ski is grippy and can make a plethora of turn shapes, plus less weight in the tail is helpful for making it through the day.” The Peregrine 80’s 3D Radius Sidecut, which blends a tight turn radius underfoot with a longer radius at the rockered tip and tail, makes for a race-meets-freeride feel. At slow speeds, testers noted the tail takes work to release. “It’s not the liveliest at the exit of the turn,” said Jon Sexauer, a 5-foot-7 expert skier. “But put the work in, and the ski really engages and carves well.” Lengths: 145, 152, 159, 166 cm
Dimensions: 125-75-109 mm Pros and Cons
+ Good combo of dampness and responsiveness
+ Transitions well between short and long turns
– Chatters underfoot in firm conditions
– Only offered in four sizes, up to 166 cm Multitasking comes naturally to some, and that includes the Atomic Cloud Q14 Revoshock S, which moves seamlessly between long and short turns. Deemed an all-mountain carver by testers, the 75-millimeter-waisted ski favors East and West Coast skiers alike who like to mix things up. “It’s a balanced beauty,” said Marina Knight, a 5-foot-5 expert skier. “It can both smear easy turns and make higher-tempo carves for those channeling their inner Mikaela Shiffrin.” In fact, the Cloud Q14 Revoshock S uses the same stainless-steel, vibration-eating technology that’s straight from Shiffrin’s race skis. Though this groomer ski has great turn-shape versatility, testers gave it lower scores for forgiveness, detecting chatter underfoot when conditions got firmer and faster. The Cloud Q14 Revoshock S comes in only four lengths, but according to Lauren Engle, a 5-foot-4 hardgoods buyer, you can size down. “Even in a 159-centimeter length, typically short for me, this ski felt totally solid.” Lengths: 156, 163, 170, 177, 184 cm
Dimensions: 128-78-112 mm Pros and Cons
+ Very stable at speed
+ Holds a consistent edge on any pitch
– Very damp
– Hooky, sluggish skidding a turn The Porsche Macan of the group, the Head Supershape e-Rally struck testers as a smooth yet agile SUV. With Head’s directive to “bring race to piste,” the Supershape e-Rally rivaled our “Best in Test” ski for the highest score in stability at speed, with hard-snow integrity a close second. “It’s a dependable ride and a ripping groomer ski that handles any turn radius you ask of it,” said Tommy Flitton, a Utah-based ski coach. With a World Cup Sandwich Cap construction that includes wood, graphene, Titanal and carbon, the e-Rally channels a Master’s race-ski vibe, with a GS turn radius and strong edge hold. Just don’t expect a playful, quick turner: according to testers, the one-track-mind, directional e-Rally is damp and feels sluggish in a skidded turn. But for intermediates through experts who prioritize dependability and edge hold over rebound energy, this ski will deliver consistent performance on any pitch. See how the best carving skis of 2027 stack up in SKI’s individual scoring criteria. Carving skis are the narrow-waisted skis designed for on-piste skiing. Carving skis typically feature waist widths below 85 millimeters. With more exaggerated side cuts (hourglass shape) than you’ll find on wider skis, carving skis are designed to chew up corduroy and hardpack snow as well as make short radius slalom turns or long arcing GS turns. It used to be that only the best skiers could handle the race-inspired skis available in the narrowest of waist widths. These stiff and demanding carving skis tended to be unapproachable to intermediates and advanced skiers looking to improve their technique. But that’s no longer the case. Featuring more tip rocker, wider shovels, and lighterweight construction materials than carving skis of the past, many models now allow strong intermediates to experience the locked-in feeling and power of these narrow-waisted skis. Our top carving ski of 2027 is the Stöckli Montero AX. It outperformed all the other carving skis we tested in Deer Valley, Utah. Testers raved about its carving ability on groomed terrain, its precision on edge, and its smooth feeling underfoot. For 2027, our testers named the Rossignol Arcade W 84 the best carving ski for women. Our female testers appreciated its precision, dependability, and carving abilities. Carving skis give it away in the name: they’re built to arc carved turns on groomed terrain. Think race skis, but made more accessible to the everyday skier. Frontside skis can be just as reliable on groomers and hardpack, even with a little added tip rocker. But because frontside skis are typically a little straighter from tip to tail with a slightly wider waist, they don’t have the same innate carving capabilities as carving skis. Where frontside skis win out is in the versatility department—they’re designed to perform even off the groomers. In short: Carving skis are the scalpels of skis, designed to be handled by an experienced hand and leave precise incisions on the snow. A frontside ski is more like a machete—it’s still sharp and effective but doesn’t require you to be as precise in your cutting. In truth, most skis are unisex and not gender-specific. Many brands produce the ski with the exact same construction technologies for both genders, but often create two different top sheets/graphics to appeal to men vs. women. In general, men and women can use the same ski but may want to choose different lengths depending on their height, weight, and their skiing style/ability. A handful of brands design true women’s skis with construction tweaks for female physiology. These skis generally come in shorter lengths (from 170 cm down to 150 cm) and use slightly softer, lighter construction materials. As a general rule of thumb, the shorter the ski, the easier it is to turn and control. So if you’re a beginner, reach for a ski that’s about chin-height. More advanced skiers often choose skis that are as long as they are tall, since longer skis provide more stability at speed and float in deep snow. So the best ski length for you will depend on your height, your skill level, and what type of skiing you hope to do. A ski-shop employee can help point you in the right direction. Note that ski length is relative. Narrow carving skis tend to ski longer than their length because they feature more effective edge, while powder skis tend to ski shorter than their length because they feature more rocker in the tip and tail. At the 2026 SKI Test in Deer Valley, Utah, 18 experienced skiers from across the country tested 26 carving skis in real-world resort conditions. To reduce subjectivity, all testers skied each model on the same day, in the same conditions, and submitted digital scorecards evaluating each ski across nine criteria: When judging the best carving skis, we place the greatest emphasis on hard-snow integrity, carving, and responsiveness—three key indicators of a top-tier carving ski. The seven winners on this list earned consistently high marks across all categories, especially those three. The skis included in the “More Skis We Recommend” section are models that excel in specific areas like playfulness or forgiveness, offering strong alternatives for skiers with specific performance preferences. Learn more about our testing methodology and scoring criteria here. Our ski reviews are the result of the largest, most rigorous on-snow test in the industry. We never charge brands to participate and don’t guarantee coverage—our annual SKI Test is a fully independent editorial project designed to deliver objective, in-depth reviews. Our expert testers include ski instructors, ski patrollers, ski shop owners, hardgoods buyers, ski technicians, and race and freeride coaches. We handpick this crew for their professional expertise and intentionally include a range of body types, ages, and home mountains to reflect the broader ski community. Bottom line: There’s no pay-to-play here—just honest feedback from people who know skis. Meet some of our veteran testers below: Crabtree spent every winter weekend brown-bagging lunch and skiing bell to bell in New Hampshire and ski racing around New England’s storied race hills. After a stint on the Bates College alpine ski team, she headed west to coach at Ski Club Vail, and then moved to the mountains above Boulder to get her Masters at the University of Colorado. An internship at SKI lead to eight years as an editor and director of the women’s ski test. She has been testing and writing about skis, boots, and gear since 1999. Born and raised in Salt Lake City, Flitton joined the Snowbird ski team as a young racer at the age of 7. He worked his way through the ranks as a racer, spending time at a ski academy in Vermont before returning to his favorite mountain in Utah. Now he spends his time coaching young freeriders how to send it big at Snowbird. He’s a veteran gear tester who has tested skis for SKI, Outside, and Powder. Loomans grew up in Mukwonago, Wisc., and took up skiing at Alpine Valley Resort. He was an USCSA All-American skier for the University of Minnesota. Translation: He knows how to bend a ski.

The hackathon brings together GS employees to propose ideas using AI, from in-house productivity improvements to broader business innovations. A total of 923 people are expected to participate through Tuesday — 797 employees from GS affiliates and 126 external participants — making it the largest edition to date. Cumulative participation over the past five years has reached 2,732. This year's theme is "Play with Gen AI Season 3: Build and Act," reflecting a dual focus on creating AI-powered outputs that actually work (Build) and connecting them to real workplaces and business operations (Act). GS Group Chairman Heo Tae-soo, who attended the event, said ideas from employees who know the workplace best, combined with AI, had become a force for changing how industrial safety is managed. "I will actively support the challenges that began at the hackathon so they can take root beyond GS, reach more workplaces and lead to new value," he said. "I hope you spend the next two days asking questions freely, taking on challenges and discovering new possibilities," he said. This year's participants are working with AI-ready data. Applying AI to industrial settings requires data to be organized in a format that AI can read — a step that must come first. Even when data has accumulated on-site, inconsistent formats and standards make retrieving and processing it time-consuming. To ease this bottleneck, GS has been refining and structuring data gathered across various business sites, including power plants and convenience stores. Its innovation unit 52g, for example, has organized tacit knowledge from GS Donghae Power — covering operations, maintenance and facilities — into AI-readable form, and is developing a power-plant-specific AI model that understands on-site knowledge and work procedures. At this hackathon, participants are combining AI-ready data with GS's AI transformation platform MISO to solve real workplace problems. The key is cutting the time spent on data preparation so ideas can be implemented faster and deployed on-site sooner. Kim Jin-a, a GS executive director who helped organize the hackathon, said five years of the event had established GS's field-centered AI transformation as an innovation model that drives real change, beyond slogans or one-off experiments. "We plan to support this year's outputs through verification and refinement so they translate into tangible results in actual work and business performance," she said. Meanwhile, the safety management AI agent team AIR (AI Risk Assessment) received the Open Innovation Award at the event. AIR originated from an idea proposed at the 3rd GS Group Hackathon by five employees from GS Power's safety and mechanical divisions. Users enter a task name and a brief description, and the AI automatically identifies potential hazards, assigns risk ratings and suggests preventive safety measures. Built by frontline workers rather than professional developers using MISO, it is now in use at more than 330 worksites, including small and midsize businesses.

GS Engineering & Construction Develops "Field-Oriented AI Solutions" Through In-House Competition GS Engineering & Construction announced on September 21 that it had selected 12 projects with high potential for on-the-job application through its in-house artificial intelligence (AI) competition, "AX Recipe," which has been ongoing since June, and held the final round. title: GS Engineering & Construction holds AI competition finals, eyes real-world deployment - 헤럴드경제
content: Over 90 teams competed; 700-plus employees trained and coached Top prize goes to AI solution for reviewing plant steel shop drawings GS Engineering & Construction is accelerating its digital transformation by moving beyond company-wide AI training to deploying employee-developed AI solutions in actual construction work. The company announced Monday that it had selected 12 projects with strong real-world applicability through its in-house AI competition, AX Recipe, and held the finals Friday. At the finals, 12 teams demonstrated AI solutions they had developed themselves. Voting by management, including CEO Heo Yun-hong, and employees determined the top three teams. This year's top prize went to an AI solution for streamlining the review of plant steel shop drawings. The winning entry replaced a manual process of visually cross-checking thousands of steel members one by one with an AI-based solution, cutting review time by more than 80 percent and significantly improving accuracy. The representative of the winning team will receive an invitation to attend CES 2027, the world's largest consumer electronics and IT trade show. Now in its second year, AX Recipe — launched last year — is GS Engineering & Construction's flagship innovation program in which employees use AI to solve real workplace problems. This year the format shifted from individual to team participation, yielding a broad range of practical AI solutions ready for immediate deployment across the company's business lines, including architecture, infrastructure and plant construction, going well beyond simple task automation. More than 90 teams entered the competition, and some 700 employees received AI training and dedicated coaching over July and August. The finals showcased a variety of construction-specific ideas, including a defect-prevention platform integration solution for the design and construction phases, a project contract change tracking system, and a solution for cross-checking 3D design models against specifications. GS Engineering & Construction plans to review the top projects for broader rollout across divisions and the company before applying them to operations in stages. "Through AX Recipe, we confirmed that our employees can go beyond learning about AI to actually applying it on the job and delivering tangible results," a company official said. "We will continue to strengthen a system that organically connects training, hands-on practice and real-world application, and we will keep expanding a data and AI utilization model tailored to the construction industry." Meanwhile, GS Engineering & Construction posted operating profit of 232.4 billion won ($168 million) in the first half of this year, up 41.8 percent from 164.2 billion won in the same period last year.

title: GS Retail awards scholarships to 47 consumer studies students - 헤럴드경제
content: 75 million won distributed; cumulative total reaches 1.2 billion won over 18 years GS Retail held the "2026 GS Shop Consumer Leader Scholarship Certificate Ceremony" at GS Gangseo N Tower in Yeongdeungpo-gu, Seoul, on Friday, awarding 75 million won ($54,300) in scholarships to 47 undergraduate and graduate students majoring in consumer studies at 12 universities nationwide. Each of the 38 undergraduate recipients received 1.5 million won, while each of the nine graduate students received 2 million won. The ceremony was attended by Bae Jae-seong, head of GS Retail's home shopping business unit support division, Korea Consumer Affairs Association President Lee Hye-mi, Secretary General Song Yu-jin, and scholarship committee members Kim Seong-suk and Lee Seong-rim, who offered words of encouragement to the recipients. GS Retail has run the GS Shop Consumer Leader Scholarship Program since 2009 to support students majoring in consumer studies. The program is sponsored by GS Retail and organized by the Korean Society of Consumer Policy and Education and the Korea Consumer Affairs Association. Including this year's 47 recipients, the program has supported a cumulative total of 832 students with 1.2 billion won in scholarships. This year, GS Retail also launched a home shopping studio tour program for scholarship recipients for the first time, giving them a chance to experience the retail and home shopping industry firsthand and deepen their understanding of the field. "Supporting the growth of consumer affairs professionals is an important part of ESG management, and we will continue to back the development of future talent," Bae said.

title: [INTERVIEW] Authentic Korean convenience meals attract foreigners - The Korea Times
content: Min Jung-hwan of GS Retail says Korean convenience store dosirak are drawing foreigners because they want authentic Korean-style meals. GS25 is expanding offerings with banchan such as bulgogi, dakgangjeong and japchae, while keeping prices generally under 7,000 won. The company says demand is being driven by lunchflation, better quality and more varied recipes. GS25 also says it launches new dosirak through consumer surveys, testing and a roughly 12-week production process. Min Jung-hwan, a merchandiser with GS Retail’s Fresh Food Team, poses next to the company’s logo at their headquarters in Gangnam District, Seoul, Sept. 7. Courtesy of GS Retail The global popularity of Korean food has reached a point where convenience store meal boxes, known as “dosirak,” have become part of a new market trend where signature Korean flavors and traditional recipes have become a hit with international visitors and popular in new markets. Min Jung-hwan, who plans and oversees dosirak production for GS25 at GS Retail’s Merchandise Headquarters, is seeing the shift firsthand. Rather than creating separate products for foreign customers, the retailer is increasingly offering the same dosirak that appeal to Korean consumers, reflecting growing interest in authentic Korean flavors. “We don’t make dosirak that are specially for foreigners because many of them like what Koreans enjoy. Even at GS25 stores in Vietnam and Mongolia, visitors are interested in authentic Korean-style dosirak. We try to meet such expectations so that they can feel they are inside a Korean convenience store,” Min said in an interview with The Korea Times. “To serve the rising number of foreigners coming to Korea, we are boosting a pipeline for those with banchan (side dishes) they usually like, including bulgogi (marinated meat), dakgangjeong (fried chicken in sauce) or japchae (stir-fried glass noodles with vegetables).” Dosirak have continuously evolved alongside Korea’s convenience store industry, driven by their enduring popularity. The changes go beyond the quality of the food, encompassing a wider variety of banchan, more diverse packaging and a growing focus on the tastes and needs of a diverse group of consumers. Min Jung-hwan poses with a dosirak inside a GS25 store in Seoul, Sept. 7. Inside the store are ready-to-eat fresh food items, including dosirak, gimbap, hamburgers and sandwiches. Courtesy of GS Retail The trend is propelled in part by increased prices across retail and dine-in markets, driving the consumers to seek more affordable foods. For those who have to eat meals while on the run, convenience stores have become an ideal spot to grab a bite, with dosirak and other fresh food items rarely exceeding 7,000 won ($5.21). Min said the trend shows that convenience store foods have evolved beyond their image as cheap, simple meals. “It is true that 'lunchflation' has heightened people’s sensitivity to how much they have to pay, so it has expanded the markets for affordable convenience store dosirak,” Min said. “What’s different now from the past is the level of quality. In the past, dosirak had to be cheap and were merely an alternative to ordinary meals. Now, they have become a popular category. They use seasonal ingredients to introduce eye-catching items like spring cabbage bibimbap. They have gotten more expensive, too, but they are still popular among those who are willing to pay for taste satisfaction. Our most popular dosirak is 6,900 won. In the past, those priced below 6,000 won sold the best.” Marketing efforts have also raised consumers’ expectations. The company has collaborated with Choi Kang-rok, the winner of the second season of Netflix’s “Culinary Class Wars,” on new dosirak. GS25 has also launched a “Dosirak of the Month” program, fueling consumer curiosity and driving sales. "Hyeja Dosirak," featuring actress Kim Hye-ja, has been one of GS25’s signature dosirak since 2010. “We launched a renewal of GS25 dosirak earlier this month. We conduct consumer surveys, and the results show that consumers’ needs keep changing. We cannot create dosirak based solely on trends or what's popular in society. We need hard data that reflects consumers’ opinions,” Min said. GS25's dosirak featuring Kim Hye-ja, left, includes five main dishes, five sides and two appetizers. GS25's No.1 Chicken Dorisak features garlic mayo chicken and spicy garlic fried chicken. Courtesy of GS Retail Launching a new dosirak starts with analyzing current market trends and planning how to target consumers, followed by deciding on the banchan and style. Culinary experts test the selected dishes and adjust their flavors to create a balanced meal. The completed sample then undergoes a “lot test” at a manufacturing plant to determine whether it is suitable for mass production. Based on feedback from the test, the final dosirak is prepared for launch. Around 20 different types of dosirak are featured each month at GS25 stores. GS Retail runs nine manufacturing plants nationwide that together distribute dosirak to 18,000 GS25 stores across Korea. The key is consistent quality and taste for all dosirak products of the same type. Launching a new dosirak usually takes about 12 weeks. Some products, such as spring cabbage bibimbap, which went viral on social media, are produced more quickly by the company to take advantage of swift moving trends. Korean dosirak, according to Min, were heavily influenced by Japanese bento back when the domestic market was small and limited. For many years, there were not even proper food containers available in Korea. “But the market has grown, and now there are more than 53,000 convenience stores. There are diverse food containers and equipment to realize a greater variety of banchan for mass production. We have built up know-how like how to bake bread to soak up different sauces or how to make dried seaweed for triangular gimbap crispier,” Min said. “We’re trying to implement automation at our plants, except placing banchan in each container because robots take a longer time for that job than humans hand-packing them.” Meet Korean 'fencing idol' Yang Seung-hye whose looks drew AI comparison YouTube ad restrictions put Korean 'mukbang' creators on alert Foreign students choose Seoul over New York, London, Paris for vibrant culture, cheaper rent: report Won-dollar rate back on roller coaster as 1,400-won mark looms How to lighten the mood at Chuseok family gatherings

title: GS Retail stock holds steady as investors watch recent earnings - AD HOC NEWS
content: GS Retail stock reflects recent earnings trends from the first half of 2026, giving investors a clearer view of its core retail and convenience business. The latest revenue and profit figures highlight both growth areas and margin pressures. GS Retail stock (ISIN KR7007070006) remains closely tied to the company’s recent earnings performance, with investors focusing on the most up-to-date revenue and profit figures from its latest reported period in 2026. As of September 20, 2026, the stock’s valuation is increasingly being viewed through the lens of these fundamentals and the broader consumer and retail environment in South Korea. For the most recent reported period in fiscal 2026, GS Retail disclosed consolidated revenue running in the hundreds of billions of KRW, underscoring the scale of its convenience store and retail operations. The latest half-year results for 2026 show that revenue for the period rose compared with the corresponding period of the prior year, reflecting both store network expansion and steady same-store sales growth. In that same reporting period, operating profit also increased versus the previous year, but at a slower pace than revenue, pointing to ongoing margin pressure from labor and logistics costs. The company’s earnings mix continues to be driven by its core convenience store segment, with food, beverage and daily-needs items accounting for the bulk of sales. Within these results, management highlighted revenue growth that outpaced the prior year by a mid-single-digit to high-single-digit percent range, while operating profit improved by a lower percent rate, illustrating the challenge of fully passing cost pressures on to consumers. Historical figures from fiscal year 2024 are now used mainly as a comparison base: in that year, GS Retail reported smaller revenue and operating profit levels than in the most recently reported 2026 period, indicating a multi-year growth trend but also showing that profit margins have not expanded in line with sales. For investors, operating margin in the latest 2026 reporting period is a key metric. The most recent figures show that operating margin remains in the low- to mid-single-digit percent range, constrained by higher input costs and ongoing investments in store refurbishment and digital services. Compared with the prior year’s margin, this represents only a modest improvement, underscoring that GS Retail’s growth is still largely volume-driven rather than margin-driven. Net profit for the most recent half-year in 2026 also increased versus the same period a year earlier, but the rise was smaller than the growth in revenue, reinforcing the picture of gradual, but not dramatic, earnings leverage. Management guidance for the remainder of fiscal 2026, as communicated alongside these latest results, points to a continued focus on cost discipline and selective store expansion. The company has indicated that it expects revenue for full-year 2026 to exceed the prior year’s level, while aiming for a slight improvement in operating margin compared with 2025. Historical guidance from fiscal year 2024 serves as a backdrop here: at that time, GS Retail’s outlook was for more moderate revenue growth and stable margins, and the subsequent actual results suggest that the company has managed to deliver somewhat better top-line momentum than originally signaled, though margin enhancement remains gradual. As of September 20, 2026, GS Retail’s market capitalization on its primary listing in South Korea reflects the cumulative impact of these earnings trends and expectations for the remainder of the year. The current valuation embeds assumptions of continued revenue growth in 2026 and a cautious improvement in profitability, with the convenience store segment remaining the central earnings driver. Compared with historical market capitalization levels in earlier years, the current figure stands higher, mirroring the company’s larger revenue base and expansion of its store network, though investors are still monitoring whether margins can improve enough to justify further rerating. From a longer-term perspective, GS Retail’s latest 2026 results and guidance suggest that the stock now trades on a balance between growth potential and cost-related risks. For investors, the most important checkpoint over the coming quarters will be whether operating margin can move meaningfully higher from its low- to mid-single-digit percent range as revenue continues to grow. If the company can demonstrate that its investments in logistics, digital platforms and store upgrades translate into better profitability, the current earnings trajectory in 2026 may support a more constructive view of GS Retail stock.
